issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness. Ambulances and pregnancy/birth reminders could fit certain illness contexts, but physical affection as a trigger is hard to reconcile without any supporting illness-related memory or appraisal content, and the three triggers together do not suggest a single coherent illness narrative.

Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/ambient danger vigilance (needing back to wall, reacting to sudden movements, constant environmental scanning), which reads more like fear of assault or attack than threat linked to life-threatening illness. With the given trauma type, this pattern is hard to explain unless supported by corresponding trauma content, which is absent.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport does not match the rest of the profile. No trigger, threat, or memory item suggests transport-related trauma cues or a reason this strategy would be central for this illness-based PTSD presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Rage on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the memory content and the illness trauma type. The memories are otherwise characterized by somatic/nonverbal reliving, while the threat pattern is hypervigilance to external attack; intense rage does not help unify these elements into one coherent formulation.

For a trauma type of life-threatening illness, ambulances and hospital smells are plausible triggers, but pregnancy/childbirth reminders are hard to reconcile unless the illness was specifically pregnancy-related; as presented, this trigger set does not describe a coherent illness-linked cue pattern.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal/assault-like hypervigilance (needing back to wall, reacting to others' sudden movements, constant environmental scanning). That pattern is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma unless the illness occurred in a highly dangerous external context, which is not supported by the other nodes.

issues.explanation: Memory items suggest poorly elaborated, body-based re-experiencing of a medical event, which fits illness trauma, but intense rage on recall is less coherent with the rest of the profile and would usually need accompanying appraisals about blame, betrayal, or mistreatment that are absent here.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport appears disconnected from the rest of the profile: no trigger or threat item involves buses/trains/crowds, and no formulation edge suggests triggers are driving this strategy. It looks like a strategy aimed at a symptom context not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of life-threatening illness, pregnancy/childbirth/babies is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the illness specifically involved pregnancy or neonatal contexts; nothing else in the profile supports that context.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by hypervigilance to interpersonal/physical attack cues (needing back to wall, reacting to others' sudden movements, scanning the room), which fits assault/combat-type danger more than illness-related trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: These threat items do not connect plausibly to the listed illness-related triggers (hospital smell, needles/medical equipment); the cross-node pattern mixes medical trauma cues with a separate attack-style threat state.

issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is possible, but here it sits oddly with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear-based medical reminders and attack-style vigilance rather than anger-related meanings or appraisals.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to link coherently to the rest of this illness-related profile, which otherwise centers on hospital/medical cues; this strategy appears to address a different trigger context not represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance to sudden movements by others is a poor fit with the selected medical/illness triggers and memories, which suggest hospital procedures and bodily trauma rather than interpersonal attack or assault-type threat.

issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall is not well supported by the other selected items or the trauma type; the surrounding profile reflects fear, bodily re-experiencing, and medical triggers rather than anger-focused meaning or appraisals.

vignette:
Ingrid Halvorsen is a 41-year-old married firefighter of Norwegian descent who presented for psychological assessment following a life-threatening illness that occurred approximately fourteen months prior to her intake appointment. Her PCL-5 score of 68 places her well within the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across the first several sessions is one of a woman whose professional identity - built on physical competence and the capacity to function under pressure - has been quietly dismantled from the inside.

Eighteen months ago, Ingrid was admitted to the intensive care unit following a rapid-onset septic infection that had gone unrecognised for several days. What began as fatigue she attributed to a demanding rotation at the station deteriorated within seventy-two hours into organ compromise, a central line placed in her neck, and a period during which her husband was told she might not survive the night. She was conscious for much of it - conscious enough to feel the cold antiseptic swabbed across her skin before each procedure, to watch the IV lines running into her arm, to hear the mechanical rhythm of monitors she could not silence. She has described lying in a position of enforced stillness, arms extended and restrained by tubing, unable to move without triggering alarms, and she has said, more than once, that she felt less like a patient and more like a body being worked on.

The memories of those days do not come to Ingrid in narrative form. She cannot tell the story the way she tells stories about fires - with a beginning, a sequence, a resolution. Instead, what returns are fragments that seem to bypass language entirely: the smell of the ward, the particular angle of a fluorescent light, the weight of a drip line pulling at the back of her hand. When these fragments surface, she does not merely remember being in that bed - she finds her arms tensing, her neck stiffening, her body resuming the position of enforced stillness as though the memory is stored not in her mind but in her musculature. The terror that accompanied the original event returns with the memory at full intensity, unchanged by the fourteen months that have passed, and this has convinced her that she has not, in any meaningful sense, recovered.

Because the memories arrive with such force and feel so physically total, Ingrid has developed a set of strategies aimed at keeping them at a distance. She redirects her attention aggressively - filling her off-shift hours with activity, refusing to allow silence, reaching for her phone or the television the moment her mind begins to drift toward anything resembling the hospital. She avoids any situation that carries emotional weight, having learned that strong feeling of any kind seems to lower whatever barrier she has constructed. Most concretely, she has declined two routine medical appointments since discharge and has begun rerouting her drive to the station to avoid passing the hospital where she was treated. These strategies have not resolved the memories, however - they have preserved them intact, unprocessed, exactly as raw as the day she was discharged, ensuring that when intrusions do break through, they carry the same undiminished terror. The avoidance has also had a professional cost: Ingrid works on a crew that responds to medical emergencies alongside paramedics, and she has twice requested reassignment away from calls flagged as medical, something her captain has noted and questioned.

Her body, meanwhile, operates as though the threat has never fully passed. She scans her environment constantly - at the station, at home, in ordinary social settings - and her physical state is one of sustained readiness that she cannot voluntarily lower. This hypervigilance means that ordinary sensory cues carry enormous weight: the antiseptic smell of a cleaning product used at the station, the sight of a colleague's blood-glucose monitor, the procedural preparation before a routine physical - each of these lands in her nervous system as a signal of danger, activating the same physical reactivity that accompanied the original crisis, which in turn makes the underlying memories feel closer and more present. The loop is one she has begun to recognise without being able to interrupt it.

What finally brought Ingrid to seek help was a mandatory occupational health review she could not avoid. She sat in the waiting room, smelled the antiseptic, and left before her name was called. She told her husband that evening, for the first time, that she was frightened she was no longer fit to do her job. What she hopes for, she said at intake, is to be able to walk back into a medical setting without her body deciding she is dying.
